Deriving high-fidelity residential building archetypes and typical usage patterns from 
national energy use surveys to enhance “initial guesses” for Urban Building Energy Model 
(UBEM) inputs 
 
Jingwen Gu1,*, Timur Dogan1 
1Environmental Systems Lab, Cornell University, Ithaca NY, United States. 
*Corresponding Author: jg2369@cornell.edu 
 
 
 
Abstract 
Solar shading simulation is an essential first step for many 
urban building energy modeling (UBEM). This paper 
introduces a novel point cloud-based solar shading 
algorithm designed to overcome the efficiency and 
scalability limitations of current shading calculation 
methods used in urban building energy modeling. 
Traditional methods, such as Energy Plus, use a polygon-
clipping or OpenGL-based pixel-counting to determine a 
surface's sunlit fraction, sky view, and horizon visibility 
and then combine these with the Perez Sky Model. At the 
same time, the Radiance Daysim or the two-phase method 
offers full, octree-accelerated ray traces that also account 
for indirect contributions. While these methods are widely 
considered state-of-the-art, they pose limitations in urban 
applications where modelers encounter large models with 
high polygon counts where computational overhead 
becomes unfeasible. In addition, modelers are often 
required to reconstruct the mesh geometry of buildings, 
terrain, and vegetation from Light Detection and Ranging 
(LiDAR) point clouds. This mesh reconstruction is 
complex and often requires a significant overhead. We 
present the Virtual Horizon Method, which can directly 
leverage LiDAR point clouds and does not require 
reconstructing the mesh geometry of the urban context. 
Instead, we rasterize the point cloud data into a height 
map with arbitrary resolution. We then query the 
heightmap for a virtual horizon line for any point of 
interest within the model. We use the virtual horizon to 
determine the visibility of the horizon line, sky dome, 
solar disc, and circumsolar region, and we use the Perez 
Sky model to compute incident radiation at a given sensor 
point.  Preliminary results show that the algorithm 
maintains high performance for high sensor density and 
large context model sizes without significantly sacrificing 
accuracy. We demonstrate that our method is orders of 
magnitude faster than a conventional radiation mapping 
workflow using Radiance and ClimateStudio while 
maintaining a mean accuracy of 94.53% for annual 
irradiance predictions, assuming a Lambertian surface 
model.

Key Innovations 
• Fast processing of LiDAR data for urban shading 
calculations. 
• Virtual horizon concept to efficiently store complex 
shading contexts at a model level. 
Practical Implications 
The method presented in this paper drastically simplifies 
and accelerates the handling of shading geometry for 
urban-scale energy simulations while maintaining a good 
accuracy of ~95%. 
Introduction 
Motivation: Urban development plays a major role in 
global carbon emissions. With approximately 29% of 
total US greenhouse gas emissions and up to 42% of 
global energy-related emissions resulting from building 
construction and operation (Leung 2018), modeling and 
constraining the carbon footprint related to urban 
buildings emerges as a necessary and effective approach 
towards sustainability. Urban Building Energy Modelling 
(UBEM) is thus important in that it quantitatively 
simulates and measures the energy consumption related to 
buildings and consequently allows for high-precision 
estimation and optimization of buildings’ environmental 
impact. 
Among the various tasks of UBEM, shading simulation is 
one of the most fundamental in that it accounts for the 
absorption, retention, and utilization of solar energy in 
urban settings. The shadows cast by terrain, vegetation, 
and other buildings and infrastructure can significantly 
impact the amount of solar radiation incident on building 
surfaces, thus altering the passive heat gain and affecting 
the building energy load. Similarly, favorable shading 
conditions are also a prerequisite for harnessing solar 
energy with photovoltaic technologies, through which the 
net energy load of buildings can be reduced. Shading 
simulation is thus an important first step for numerous 
UBEM applications. 
Due to the quantity and complexity of shading objects in 
urban 
settings, 
shading 
simulations 
are 
often 
computationally expensive. As the context window and 
the precision of input geometries scale up, many existing 
shading simulation methodologies used in energy 
modeling suffer from bottlenecks with large and complex 
contextual shaders. More efficient shading simulation

Related Work 
Traditional 
shading 
simulation 
methods 
typically 
represent shading geometries as meshes. One class of 
successful shading methods is polygon clipping, which is 
implemented in EnergyPlus. Polygon clipping projects 
shading geometries onto the sensor surface along the 
direct beam radiation direction and finds the boundary of 
the union of shadows on a potentially irregular surface 
(Hiller et al., 2000). The polygon clipping approach is 
often used in energy modeling applications due to its 
ability to compute accurate area fractions describing the 
shaded and unshaded parts of building surfaces. Many 
implementations of polygon clipping, including the 
classic Sutherland-Hodgeman Algorithm (Sutherland & 
Hodgman, 1974), require the polygons to be convex; even 
though other implementations, such as the Weiler-
Atherton Algorithm, (Weiler & Atherton, 1977) 
generalize to concave polygons, this method can 
encounter stability issues when shadows overlap 
excessively. 
Furthermore, 
polygon 
clipping 
is 
computationally expensive as the resulting shaded 
fractions must be computed for all simulation timesteps. 
A more recent line of work is pixel counting, which 
directly renders the scene and counts the number of pixels 
visible along the sensor surface in the direction of the 
incident radiation. Being a computer graphics method, 
pixel counting can be accelerated by GPUs by utilizing 
libraries such as OpenGL (Jones et al., 2012). This 
method can also easily incorporate transparency factors to 
model vegetation or transparent material (Hoover & 
Dogan, 2017). Alternatively, modelers could use ray 
tracing tools such as Radiance (G. J. Ward, 1994) to 
compute shading patterns. Ray tracing boasts high 
accuracy since it simultaneously simulates both beam 
radiation and reflected radiation and can generalize to 
arbitrary shading geometries. Acceleration data structures 
such as octrees and GPU acceleration can also be used.  
Despite their success, the methods discussed above all 
require mesh geometries as their input, which becomes a 
constraint since data for mesh representations are hard to 
collect and maintain for urban settings. On the other hand, 
Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) has emerged as a 
more 
popular 
source 
for 
urban 
3D 
geometry 
representations. By emitting laser pulses and receiving the 
reflected signal, LiDAR generates a three-dimensional 
point cloud that not only represents buildings, but also 
captures vegetation and the ground. Combined with the 
Geospatial Information System (GIS) (Biljecki et al., 
2017), LiDAR provides a holistic representation of the 
urban environment. Open-source LiDAR data is easily 
accessible online and can be downloaded as LAS files 
(New York State, n.d.), each of which represents a square 
tile of LiDAR points. The point cloud is often converted 
to Digital Surface Models (DSM), which are regular grids 
that store the point height for each cell. 
Researchers have demonstrated the usefulness of LiDAR 
data in downstream tasks such as photovoltaic potential 
assessment (Jakubiec & Reinhart, 2013; Lingfors et al., 
2018). For the specific task of shading simulation, Lukac 
et al. propose a DSM-based algorithm which, given the 
sun position, iterates through the grid and tests whether 
each cell shades the sensor cell by simply computing the 
slope between the top surfaces of the cells (Lukacˇ et al., 
2013).  A more recent method called the PCB 2 phase 
method projects the LiDAR points onto the sky dome and 
uses a Support Vector Machine (SVM) to fit a segmented 
horizon line to partition the sky dome into shaded and 
visible parts. These methods are simple and fast, and taps 
into the strengths of the DSM data structure (Bognár et 
al., 2021).  
Our method is conceptually similar to these LiDAR-based 
methods but differs in ways that optimize efficiency: 
unlike the algorithm from Lukac et al., which is time-
dependent, our method only requires one pass to find the 
virtual horizon; our method also traces the DSM more 
efficiently by traversing in the direction of the incident ray 
and stopping whenever a shading object is found, thus 
avoiding traversal of the entire grid. Compared with the 
PCB 2 phase method, our method does not project the 
point cloud itself onto the sky dome, which is 
prohibitively costly if the sensor sample size is large; 
instead, we only project the top of each cell, thus enabling 
the method to handle larger LiDAR contexts and more 
sensors. We are also the first to employ the algorithm on 
a city-scale LiDAR tile, thus demonstrating the efficiency 
and scalability of our method. 
Methods 
In this section, we describe the Virtual Horizon Method 
as a 2.5D raytracing algorithm. We explain the 
rasterization of LiDAR points into a height map. Finally, 
we present the ray tracing method to traverse the height 
map and discuss how shading results can be used in 
subsequent workflows, including irradiance calculations, 
which is essential for photovoltaic simulation and other 
UBEM tasks.

LiDAR point representation for urban landscapes 
LiDAR data is efficient to collect and update for large 
urban areas. The resultant point clouds are typically 
widely available (i.e. full coverage for the US that can be 
obtained from USGIS Lidar Explorer (USGIS, 2024).  
Aerial LiDAR sample points along the top surface of the 
terrain. LiDAR point clouds are a 2.5D representation that 
compresses the 3D information by only capturing the 
height of the top-most surface of any object. This leaves 
out any substructure beneath the surface, such as cavities, 
tunnels, or cantilevered spaces. This, however, can be 
sufficient to reconstuct building envelopes and shading 
geometry for  Urban Building Energy Modelling. 
The heightmap data structure 
The intuition behind the heightmap data structure is that 
it matches the way LiDAR data is collected. Since LiDAR 
points are a 2.5D geometric representation, they can be 
further rasterized into a 2D array whose two axes parallel 
the N-S/E-W axes and whose values represent the heights 
of the corresponding terrain slices. This data structure is 
easier to ray trace through and further compresses the 
memory footprint of the LiDAR point cloud into a 
workable size. 
Since each heightmap array cell may correspond to 
multiple LiDAR points, this data structure also requires a 
function to map multiple point inputs to a single height 
for the cell. We experimented with simple functions such 
as taking the maximum, minimum, or average height of 
all LiDAR points contained in the cell, among which the 
maximum function proved to be the most effective.

dataset (.las file) with equations (1) (2):

Raytracing through the height map

top-most surface, for raytracing, we also assume that each 
cell represents a solid box whose footprint is the same 
square as the cell and whose height is stored inside the 
cell. This greatly simplifies the ray tracing process.

Experiments 
In this section, we evaluate the speed and accuracy of the 
Virtual Horizon Method under different shading 
geometry and sensor point settings. We first compare the 
maximum elevations 𝜙𝜙෨ returned by VHM to the ground 
truth elevations, which we compute using ray-mesh 
intersections in Rhinoceros3D. To quantify the elevation 
errors' significance, we then use the elevations in the 
irradiance computation workflow using the Perez Sky 
Model and compare the PV yield errors. We also 
demonstrate the scalability of VHM by applying it to a 
full LAS tile in Ithaca, NY to compute irradiance at a 4 
sensor/m2 resolution. Finally, we present ablation studies 
to tune hyperparameters and test out different 
implementation details. 
Simple Geometry Test: We first randomly created 
simple geometries in CAD as shown in Figure 4. and 
randomly sampled points along their top surfaces to 
simulate LiDAR point clouds. We also sampled 7 sensor 
points near the geometries. The point data is then input to 
VHM where the heightmap is created from the simulated 
LiDAR point cloud and raytraced with respect to each of 
the 7 sensor points. To obtain the corresponding ground 
truth, we randomly sampled points along a unit sphere 
around each sensor to represent the ray directions. We 
then used the “Ray|Mesh” intersection component in 
Rhinoceros3D/ Grasshopper to check whether each ray 
intersects with some shading geometry. The rays are then 
put in 360 azimuth bins, and the maximum intersecting 
elevation is identified. We compare this value with the 
raytraced maximum intersecting elevation from VHM 
and find that the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is 0.2027 
radians. Figure 5 shows the virtual horizon graphs that 
compare our heightmap-based method with a fully 
raytraced VH using 3D CAD geometry.

Irradiance comparison 
To quantitatively gauge the impact of the maximum 
elevation prediction error from VHM on downstream 
tasks, we input the estimated predictions to the Perez Sky 
Model algorithm to compute the hourly irradiance 
estimations for each sensor point at all 8760 hours of the 
year. For evaluation, we compared the irradiance 
prediction accuracy against two different ground truths. 
The first is the irradiance simulation from Climate Studio 
(Solemma, n.d.), which is a Rhino/Grasshopper (McNeel, 
n.d.) plugin using Radiance (G. Ward, n.d.) for shading 
computation. The second is using the ground truth 
altitudes 
obtained 
by 
directly 
doing 
Ray|Mesh 
intersection in Rhino (as described in section 3.1) and 
feeding them into the Perez Sky Model (Perez et al., 
1993).  
We provide the second comparison in order to quantify 
the impact of the altitude prediction error on downstream 
tasks such as irradiance computation and decouple it from 
the error introduced by the Perez Sky Model itself. This is 
because Climate Studio’s irradiance simulation accounts 
for reflections and ambient contributions, the Perez Sky 
Model simplifies irradiance computation by only 
computing the direct radiation and diffuse radiation from 
the skydome, the horizon, and the circum-solar disk. We 
first computed the hourly irradiance by feeding the 
ground truth maximum elevation predictions obtained 
from Grasshopper into the Perez Sky Model algorithm 
and compared the results with our predictions.  
We found that compared with the ground truth elevation-
Perez Sky irradiance estimates, VHM-Perez Sky has an 
accuracy of 99.48%; whereas compared with the 
ClimateStudio ground truth the accuracy is 94.53%. Both 
demonstrate that VHM propagates relatively small errors 
to downstream tasks such as irradiance computation. We 
show the hourly irradiance map of a random sensor point

Full-scale ray tracing and irradiance computation 
The strongest advantage of VHM is its efficiency and 
capability to handle large terrain models and high sensor 
point density. To demonstrate this, we loaded in the entire 
u_3750069950 LiDAR tile, which represents a square 
area roughly 1700 meters in diameter, and uniformly 
sampled sensor points at different densities. Since we are 
interested in rooftop irradiance computation, we culled 
out sensors that belonged to cells classified as buildings. 
We set the sensor tilt and azimuth such that the sensor 
plane is roughly parallel to the underlying terrain.  
At 4-meter spacing, we were able to build the heightmap, 
run VHM ray tracing, and compute irradiance predictions 
in 584.366 seconds. This is an enormous improvement on 
standard shading and energy modelling tools such as 
ClimateStudio or LadyBug, which simply cannot load 
sensor point volumes and terrain models at this scale 
within a reasonable timeframe. 
In Figure 11, we show the computed irradiance map, 
where the color of each pixel represents the annual 
cumulative irradiance of the corresponding sensor.

Discussion 
In our experiments, we found that the accuracy of VHM 
is relatively small. It is shown that in general, decreasing 
the grid size improves both the Mean Absolute Error in 
predicted maximum altitude and the accuracy of the 
predicted irradiance, but once cell size decreases beyond 
0.5m the error increases instead. We hypothesize that this 
is because smaller cell sizes produce a more detailed 
DSM, but as cell sizes decrease beyond the sampling 
density of LiDAR points themselves, the lack of sufficient 
data becomes irrecoverable by the simple interpolation 
method. It is unclear whether a more sophisticated 
interpolation method may further reduce the optimal cell 
size. Because the observed latency is roughly proportional 
to the square of the cell size, we advise using the 0.5m cell 
size. 
Regarding the accuracy of predicted annual irradiance, we 
find that the minimum irradiance accuracy compared with 
Climate Studio is 94.53%, whereas the minimum 
irradiance accuracy compared with ground truth altitude 
+ Perez Sky Model is 99.48%. This suggests that the error 
introduced by altitude prediction error is sufficiently 
small, and the overall error of the pipeline is small even 
with a simple irradiance model such as the Perez Sky 
Model. In particular, since irradiance models are known 
to be unstable, some reaching more than 5% errors 
themselves, the error introduced by VHM is not of great 
significance. Furthermore, we observe that for all cell 
sizes, there is a constant 5% gap between the irradiance 
errors from the two ground truths, which is most probably 
due to the Perez Sky Model itself. Using a more 
sophisticated irradiance model may be able to further 
reduce our error from Radiance, which we leave for future 
work to validate. 
With this relatively small sacrifice in accuracy, VHM has 
many strengths compared with conventional methods

such as polygon clipping, pixel counting, and 3D ray-
tracing. VHM is very fast and enables almost real-time 
irradiance computation for building-scale inputs. It is also 
able to take an entire 1500m×1500m LiDAR tile as input 
and compute annual irradiance for sensors generated at 
0.5-meter spacing in under 188 minutes, whereas most 
conventional methods virtually cannot handle inputs at 
this scale within a reasonable time window. For instance, 
the Climate Studio simulation is only designed for 
building-scale simulation, and even though one could 
break large urban contexts into smaller tiles and run 
simulations on each, the process is still labor-intensive 
and takes more time than VHM. VHM thus unlocks the 
possibility to carry out UBEM under massive input size 
and tight time constraints at a minimal cost.  
Moreover, by using LiDAR point clouds instead of 
meshes as geometric representations, VHM utilizes data 
sources that are much more accessible and easier to 
maintain, especially on an urban scale. In addition, VHM 
can still be applied to conventional mesh representations, 
where we sample the maximum height of mesh 
geometries at regular spacing. We leave more extensive 
experimentation and optimization of mesh-based VHM 
for future work. 
We acknowledge that VHM still has many limitations. 
The heightmap data structure can become memory-
intensive for larger input sizes, and we hypothesize that it 
can be optimized with more efficient data structure and 
algorithm designs. Whereas VHM is easily parallelizable 
across threads, unlike pixel counting, it is still unclear 
how VHM can be even further accelerated by GPUs. 
Moreover, the heightmap data structure limits the 
expressiveness of geometric representation, most notably 
undercuts. VHM also does not differentiate between 
building and vegetation data and does not account for 
transparency and temporal variability of shading objects. 
We hypothesize that these problems can be mitigated by 
extending VHM to a voxel-based method, which we also 
leave for future work. 
Consequently, we advise that VHM be used as a 
simulation tool for early-stage design and planning due to 
its efficiency and suitability for large geometric context 
size. For more in-depth and precise UBEM tasks, 
however, it is probably more desirable to fall back to 
mainstream tools such as Radiance for higher accuracy 
considerations. 
Conclusion 
In this paper, we proposed Virtual Horizon Method, a fast 
LiDAR-based ray tracing algorithm suitable for UBEM 
tasks. By taking LiDAR point clouds as input, this method 
taps into the accessibility and affordability of LiDAR 
compared to mesh representations of geometries and also 
enables shading simulation at a much larger scale than 
conventional methods would allow. 
We find that by utilizing LiDAR data and intelligently 
designing data structures, it is possible to accurately 
represent urban geometries and efficiently perform 
shading computations without incurring significant errors 
in downstream tasks. Through our experiments, we 
demonstrated that the method achieves very low latency 
while sacrificing only a small error in the shading 
prediction, with the MAE of VHM’s maximum elevation 
prediction being 0.0724 radians. We also showed that this 
error has an almost negligible effect on the accuracy of 
downstream tasks such as irradiance simulation, where 
our method still achieves an accuracy of 94.53%. 
Moreover, we find that VHM is easy to integrate with 
downstream workflows and that it is possible to take an 
entire 1500m×1500m LiDAR tile as input and compute 
the annual irradiance of all roof surfaces with sensors 
placed at 0.5-meter intervals within a reasonable time 
window, whereas conventional methods struggle with 
handling input data of such scale, thus opening up the 
possibility of fast urban-scale ray tracing.  
Our main contribution consists of the Virtual Horizon 
Method, which offers a faster counterpart to conventional 
shading simulation tools and enables users to perform 
shading computation and irradiance simulation on much 
larger contexts than conventional methods. 
In terms of limitation and future work, we also note that 
VHM has much room for optimization and that it can be 
extended to voxel-based data structures in order to 
represent the input geometry more accurately and account 
for other parameters, such as the transparency and 
temporal variability of the shading objects. Besides 
irradiance prediction, we also anticipate future work that 
adapts our shading prediction workflow to other 
downstream tasks such as photovoltaic yield predictions, 
daylight and glare simulations, and thermal comfort 
simulations.

Abstract: Solar shading simulation is an essential first step for many urban building energy modeling (UBEM). This paper introduces a novel point cloud-based solar shading algorithm designed to overcome the efficiency and scalability limitations of current shading calculation methods used in urban building energy modeling. Traditional methods, such as Energy Plus, use a polygon- clipping or OpenGL-based pixel-counting to determine a surface's sunlit fraction, sky view, and horizon visibility and then combine these with the Perez Sky Model. At the same time, the Radiance Daysim or the two-phase method offers full, octree-accelerated ray traces that also account for indirect contributions. While these methods are widely considered state-of-the-art, they pose limitations in urban applications where modelers encounter large models with high polygon counts where computational overhead becomes unfeasible. In addition, modelers are often required to reconstruct the mesh geometry of buildings, terrain, and vegetation from Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds. This mesh reconstruction is complex and often requires a significant overhead. We present the Virtual Horizon Method, which can directly leverage LiDAR point clouds and does not require reconstructing the mesh geometry of the urban context. Instead, we rasterize the point cloud data into a height map with arbitrary resolution. We then query the heightmap for a virtual horizon line for any point of interest within the model. We use the virtual horizon to determine the visibility of the horizon line, sky dome, solar disc, and circumsolar region, and we use the Perez Sky model to compute incident radiation at a given sensor point. Preliminary results show that the algorithm maintains high performance for high sensor density and large context model sizes without significantly sacrificing accuracy. We demonstrate that our method is orders of magnitude faster than a conventional radiation mapping workflow using Radiance and ClimateStudio while maintaining a mean accuracy of 94.53% for annual irradiance predictions, assuming a Lambertian surface model.
